layers.name: Application
layers.sub: the task, the sensor that feeds it, and the form the input takes

layers.name: Computation
layers.sub: the neuron and its execution contract

layers.name: Software stack
layers.sub: train, then export, compile, and run, in process order

buckets.name: conventional
buckets.meaning: The claim's target is a conventional processor, whatever software steps the network.

buckets.name: simulated
buckets.meaning: The claim's target is a model of neuromorphic hardware that is not the silicon.

buckets.name: neuromorphic
buckets.meaning: The claim's target is fabricated neuromorphic silicon, or a custom spiking accelerator on an FPGA measured as its own target.

code.title: Input encoding and readout
code.text: Nearly all modern low-T conversion feeds the real-valued image as constant current, which makes layer one effectively an ANN layer. Readout cost and the decision window are rarely inside the reported measurement.

compute.title: Time model
compute.text: T means a different thing under a synchronous tick, an asynchronous event stream, and analog continuous time. Software timesteps do not map one to one onto hardware steps.

compute.title: Per-layer horizons
compute.text: No framework expresses a per-layer timestep horizon in one forward pass. TrueNorth, Loihi, Loihi 2 and Tianjic all advance through a single global barrier.

sw.title: Operator coverage
sw.text: lava_exchange dispatches only Linear, Conv2d, AvgPool2d and Flatten. Speck has no BatchNorm operator, so the DynapCNN mapper folds it into the preceding layer. Akida caps Dense input at 57,334 features and requires bounded ReLU.

sw.title: Reset semantics
sw.text: The sharpest seam. Conversion requires reset by subtraction, worth roughly twenty accuracy points. NIR does not distinguish it from reset to a value. SpikingJelly rejects it at both export paths. Loihi needs a two-compartment workaround that doubles neuron count.

left.title: Accuracy
left.text: What every reduction below trades against, and the reason the conversion literature exists.

left.title: Latency
left.text: Set by the time model, the horizon T, and how much spike traffic the fabric carries per inference.

left.title: Energy
left.text: Static and leakage power dominate measured energy on synchronous chips, so cutting T does not cut energy proportionally.

left.title: Availability
left.text: A chip you cannot obtain is a different answer from a chip that does not suit. Access gates and dormant toolchains belong on this axis.

right.title: Measurement
right.text: A SynOps figure is an operation-count ratio under an unstated hardware model, not joules. Boundary choices alone produce 14x swings for the identical chip and network.

right.title: Toolchain decay
right.text: SNN Toolbox last released March 2021. Intel archived all Lava repositories on 13 May 2026 with no maintenance and no patches accepted. The only toolchain that reached silicon is dormant.

right.title: Portability
right.text: NIR reaches nine simulators and five hardware platforms, turning m x n integrations into m + n. Its primitive set still does not distinguish the one semantics this literature depends on from reset to a value.

right.title: Two populations
right.text: The division of labor that no survey states. Algorithm papers advance accuracy at low T and do not deploy; none of the algorithm-population records reaches physical silicon, and Section 13.6, Population Counts, counts them. Every confirmed instance of a new method reaching silicon abandons rate coding.

snntoolbox-loihi1.name: SNN Toolbox to Loihi 1
snntoolbox-loihi1.story: A rate-coded converted MobileNet measured on physical Loihi 1 silicon at CIFAR-10 scale, reaching 8.52% error on 861 cores across 7 chips.
snntoolbox-loihi1.note: Historical. SNN Toolbox was last released on PyPI (0.6.0) in March 2021, its last GitHub release tag is v0.5.0 of June 2020, and its last code commit was in August 2022; the repository is not archived and took README-only commits in January 2023. Soft reset is an optional mode in the Intel bridge, not its default (reset_mode falls back to 'hard'), it doubles the compartments per neuron, and the paper does not state which mode the 8.52% run used, so the line draws the hard reset. NxTF is Keras-native and its host repository carries a discontinuation notice. Loihi 1 is superseded.

snntoolbox-spinnaker.name: SNN Toolbox to SpiNNaker 1
snntoolbox-spinnaker.story: A converted Keras LeNet on a physical 48-chip machine, 98.20% on MNIST at roughly 0.4 s wall-clock per sample with 15 ms of simulated activity.
snntoolbox-spinnaker.note: Nothing at CIFAR-10 scale or above was found on physical SpiNNaker silicon. The route runs the PyNN IF_curr_exp cell with a hard reset to zero and a 1000 ms membrane time constant, a current-based LIF that is effectively non-leaky over the 15 ms window. A timestep here is a timer interrupt, conventionally 1 ms, by default matched to real time.

sinabs-speck.name: Sinabs to Speck
sinabs-speck.story: The live conversion route that preserves reset by subtraction end to end, on hardware anyone can buy, measured at 3.36 us on Speck1 for a single event through nine 3x3 conv-and-pool layers at stride 1 and padding 1, pad to pad.
sinabs-speck.note: Sinabs from_model() defaults to MembraneSubtract(). Speck supports subtractive reset natively via return_to_zero=False. The IF label is the default; the optional leak is linear and driven by a slow clock. Speck has no BatchNorm operator, and DynapcnnNetwork folds BatchNorm into the preceding conv or linear layer automatically (merge_bn). A Demo Kit presold at $199, a price that comes from a June 2023 trade-press reprint of the SynSense release; no research-membership requirement is stated. Speck has no global clock, so T exists only at the raster-to-events boundary. The measured runs streamed external events and bypassed the on-die sensor, and the only classical-conversion run measured on Speck is N-MNIST at 86.17 percent; the gesture result on Speck was surrogate-gradient trained.

rockpool-xylo.name: Rockpool to Xylo
rockpool-xylo.story: Deployed quantized accuracy of 95.31 percent, with power measured on the HDK at 216 to 217 uW idle, 468 to 514 uW active and 251 to 298 uW dynamic, on audio and low-dimensional signals rather than vision.
rockpool-xylo.note: Xylo documents a synchronous time-stepped architecture with a global dt, so T here is a genuine hardware tick. Reset is by subtraction as a fixed hardware property. The measured run used a simulated audio encoder with events streamed from the host in accelerated time, so the microphone chip is documented, not exercised. The readout is the membrane potential in training and any-spike detection at test, and only the input encoder is rate-like, so no neural-code chip is drawn. Same vendor as Speck, opposite time model.

spikingjelly-lava.name: SpikingJelly to Lava to Loihi 2
spikingjelly-lava.story: The obvious modern route, and it does not complete.
spikingjelly-lava.note: The recipe drawn is SpikingJelly's rate-coding ReLU-to-IF conversion with max or percentile threshold calibration; the QCFS-based recipe's ActivationAwareIFNode is rejected by lava_exchange with NotImplementedError instead. Three independent blockers. The first is structural, since to_lava_blocks accepts a flat list, tuple or nn.Sequential while the recipe returns an FX GraphModule with VoltageScaler modules, so the converted network fails on shape before any neuron is inspected. Then lava_exchange raises ValueError("lava only supports for v_reset == 0!") at four call sites, plus an assertion in CubaLIFNode.__init__, rejecting the soft-reset neurons the rate-coding recipe produces by default. Then layer dispatch covers only Linear, Conv2d, AvgPool2d and Flatten, so a VGG MaxPool fails there; a ResNet skip connection fails for the structural reason, not in dispatch. Intel archived all Lava repositories on 13 May 2026.
spikingjelly-lava.breakWhy: The converted network fails on shape before any neuron is inspected, then its soft reset is rejected, then its layers are not dispatched. The conversion produced a network the framework’s own exporter will not accept.

spikingjelly-nxtf.name: SpikingJelly to NxTF to Loihi 1
spikingjelly-nxtf.story: Substituting the maintained framework into the route that actually reached silicon, and it does not connect.
spikingjelly-nxtf.note: The recipe drawn is SpikingJelly's rate-coding ReLU-to-IF conversion with max or percentile threshold calibration; the QCFS-based recipe's ActivationAwareIFNode is rejected by lava_exchange with NotImplementedError. NxTF inherits from the Keras Model and Layer interface. No bridge from a PyTorch SNN framework exists; SNN Toolbox ingests PyTorch ANNs through ONNX, and the only automated bridge into NxTF was specific to SNN Toolbox. The host repository carries a discontinuation notice, and INRC has redirected users to Lava since 2022. NxTF on Loihi 2 was not found.
spikingjelly-nxtf.breakWhy: NxTF is Keras-native and SpikingJelly is PyTorch. The framework boundary was only ever crossed automatically by an SNN-Toolbox-specific bridge that no longer has a maintained counterpart.

spikingjelly-nir.name: SpikingJelly to NIR
spikingjelly-nir.story: The portability route, blocked by an exporter that refuses to export what the specification does not distinguish.
spikingjelly-nir.note: The recipe drawn is SpikingJelly's rate-coding ReLU-to-IF conversion with max or percentile threshold calibration; the QCFS-based recipe's ActivationAwareIFNode is rejected by lava_exchange with NotImplementedError. NIR defines seventeen primitives, six of them neuron models (I, IF, LI, LIF, CubaLI, CubaLIF). All three spiking ones (IF, LIF, CubaLIF) document reset as v = v_reset when a spike fires, and no NIR field distinguishes reset by subtraction from reset to a value, so which one a backend applies is left to the backend. SpikingJelly nir_exchange raises NotImplementedError("NIR does not distinguish soft reset.") whenever v_reset is None, a deliberate and conservative refusal; other exporters (snnTorch, Sinabs) export the same neurons with v_reset = 0 and leave the discretization to the importer, so the block is SpikingJelly's exporter policy.
spikingjelly-nir.breakWhy: The broadest interchange format in the ecosystem does not distinguish reset by subtraction from reset to a value, and SpikingJelly’s exporter refuses rather than guess.

quantizeml-akida.name: QuantizeML to CNN2SNN to Akida
quantizeml-akida.story: A shipping commercial processor, where the conversion folds to a static threshold and the temporal dimension disappears.
quantizeml-akida.note: CNN2SNN computes y = x / act_step for Akida 1.0 layers, with a static threshold absorbing BatchNorm scale and shift, folded once at conversion time. No membrane potential carries across timesteps and no T is exposed. One paper (Ziegler et al.) describes it as squashing the rate-code approximation of ReLU into one time step, and a second (Lunghi et al.) says the converted model reduces the computation to a single time step. BrainChip states 4-bit or 8-bit quantized inputs to its layers, so the events are graded rather than binary, and no BrainChip source names a reset rule; the threshold is a static comparator applied in a single pass. Akida carries a genuine rank-order-coding lineage at its input-encoding stage, per BrainChip's own tech brief description of rank coding as an encoding scheme in which information is expressed as the time and place it occurs, but the standard QuantizeML-to-CNN2SNN route nearly all published Akida results use collapses inside hidden layers to a single-pass, order-agnostic threshold comparison, so the rank-order-coding chip drawn here names only that input stage, not order-sensitive computation carried through the converted network.

quartz-loihi.name: Quartz to Loihi 1
quartz-loihi.story: A new method that reached silicon, by abandoning rate coding for TTFS.
quartz-loihi.note: Measured static, dynamic and total power, latency and energy per inference on a physical Nahuku 32 board, compared against the published NxTF numbers on the same platform (a different board, SDK version and network). The authors’ released implementation uses nxSDK 0.9.8 directly, as its code README states, while the paper's measurements were taken with NxSDK 1.0.0. The CIFAR-10 preferred energy-delay product uses an estimated static power, and the paper's 564 uJ energy label is a unit error for about 563 mJ.

slayer-loihi2.name: Lava-DL SLAYER to Loihi 2
slayer-loihi2.story: Direct training with a vendor toolchain, reaching silicon where rate-coded conversion did not.
slayer-loihi2.note: The workload drawn is the PilotNet sigma-delta network of Shrestha et al., Table 1, a steering regression from dashboard-camera frames measured on an Oheo Gulch single-chip Loihi 2 system with Lava-DL 0.4.0 and Lava 0.8.0; the int8 network ran at 0.09 mJ per inference without I/O, 1.21 ms latency and 7403.80 samples per second. A sigma-delta ReLU unit has no membrane or reset, so no neuron or reset chip is drawn, and steering regression has no task chip. The PilotNet LIF result is a vendor tutorial notebook, not a peer-reviewed measurement. Intel moved Loihi 2 toward graded sigma-delta payloads, citing Loihi 1 experience that rate-coded converted models suffer long latencies and inter-chip congestion. An ANN-to-sigma-delta conversion (Brehove et al.) was separately measured on a 16-chip Loihi 2 board. Intel archived the Lava repositories on 13 May 2026.

spikingjelly-gpu.name: SpikingJelly to a GPU
spikingjelly-gpu.story: The framework's own benchmark, timed end to end on an NVIDIA A100, where training a Spiking ResNet-18 with surrogate gradients reached up to 11x the speed of Norse (8x over snnTorch) at T = 32 and inference at ANN2SNN-scale T up to 2x.
spikingjelly-gpu.note: A conventional target. The paper states LIF neurons at SpikingJelly defaults with hard reset to zero, fed random 3x224x224 tensors at batch size 16 with mixed precision and no dataset. The training benchmark ran SpikingJelly's CuPy-compiled LIF kernels alongside PyTorch CUDA tensor operations, so nothing about a spiking substrate is measured. Training-iteration time was taken at T = 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32, and the ANN2SNN inference run is the same LIF network timed at T = 128 to 1024 with only T = 128 reported, on an Ubuntu 18.04 server with an Intel Xeon Silver 4210R host and 256 GB of memory.

mlgenn-gpu.name: mlGeNN to GeNN to a GPU
mlgenn-gpu.story: A converted VGG-16 and ResNet-20 simulated as GeNN-generated CUDA code on a 12 GB Titan V, with rate-based and few-spike conversion both evaluated on CIFAR-10 and only few-spike conversion run at ImageNet scale, on VGG-16 and ResNet-34.
mlgenn-gpu.note: A conventional target. On CIFAR-10 the converted VGG-16 ran 2.5x faster than BindsNET, the few-spike ResNet-20 a little over 2x slower than the original TensorFlow ANN at large batch sizes (at batch size 1 the same network is 3.5x faster than the ANN), and the fastest rate-based model over 100x slower than that ANN. Rate-based conversion used T = 2500 for VGG-16 and T = 1000 for ResNet-20; few-spike conversion used K = 10 and K = 8. The IF neurons use a hard reset to zero, stated in the paper and in ml_genn 1.0's if_neurons.py.

nest-cpu.name: PyNN and NEST to a CPU cluster
nest-cpu.story: A full-scale cortical microcircuit of about 80,000 LIF neurons and 0.3 billion synapses, simulated by NEST on a 32-node Intel Xeon cluster and compared head to head with SpiNNaker in the same paper.
nest-cpu.note: A conventional target. NEST runtime saturated around 3x real time with hybrid MPI and multithreading, and its lowest total energy came at about 144 threads and a 4.6x slowdown, where NEST and SpiNNaker had comparable energy per synaptic event. NEST used a 0.1 ms integration step. A separate performance report scales a later NEST-5g development build (a May 2017 snapshot) running the hpc_benchmark balanced random network from an SLI script under weak scaling to 82,944 nodes of the K computer, not the NEST 2.8 PyNN microcircuit run; there the connect phase stays near 80 seconds while prepare and run grow with node count. Not a classification workload; the record names no dataset, neural code or learning rule.

ttfs-cortex-m4.name: TTFS conversion to a Cortex-M4 MCU
ttfs-cortex-m4.story: A quantized 8-bit CNN converted with time-to-first-spike encoding among others and deployed on the ARM Cortex-M4 MCU, where Table 1 reports 48 microjoules and about 6 ms per inference at 87.9%, with the task unstated, against an analog Innatera chip in the same paper.
ttfs-cortex-m4.note: A conventional target. Energy, latency and accuracy were read with an external power analyzer under the MLPerf Tiny windowed protocol. The 8-bit CNN on the same MCU took 60 microjoules at 89.5%, and the same network on the Innatera SNP analog chip 24 microjoules and about 0.8 ms at 88.2%, so the energy reduction is 20 percent by the paper's own numbers, where the paper writes 23. The paper names TTFS among other encodings and also firing-rate control, and never states which encoding the measured digital SNN used. The pipeline is the paper's own, with layer-wise normalization and threshold calibration; CMSIS-NN is named only as a comparator framework, SNN Toolbox is not mentioned, and the part number is not named. The paper names CIFAR-10 and Google Speech Commands as example benchmarks and an 8-bit MobileNetV2 as its example architecture, but Table 1 is attributed to none of them, so no task chip is drawn. The source is weak in stated ways, a proposed evaluation framework whose Table 1 holds round values without the promised confidence intervals, gives latency as 6.00 ms and 6.1 ms in different sections, and states no neuron model or timestep count.

fenn-riscv.name: FeNN vector program to a RISC-V soft core
fenn-riscv.story: A recurrent spiking spoken-digit classifier stepped by a custom RISC-V vector instruction set on a soft core synthesized onto a Kria KV260 FPGA, reported significantly faster than a similar model on Loihi and twice as fast as an embedded GPU at half the energy.
fenn-riscv.note: A conventional target in this survey's vocabulary, a programmable RISC-V processor rather than a fixed-function spiking accelerator, even though it is realized on an FPGA. FeNN uses adaptive LIF neurons with subtractive reset and 16-bit fixed-point arithmetic with stochastic rounding. The SNN itself is RISC-V assembly emitted by a host-side C++ JIT assembler on the Kria's Cortex-A53; Vivado synthesizes the soft core once. The Loihi comparison is against the time Rao et al. report for a similar ALIF RSNN on Loihi, not a measurement in the FeNN paper, and the energy comparison is whole-board mains energy of the KV260 against a Jetson Orin Nano, both under desktop Linux. The SHD input is cochlea-model spike trains. FeNN-DMA, the follow-on system-on-chip, measured simulation throughput of a balanced random network of up to 16,000 neurons from on-chip performance counters and accuracy on Spiking Heidelberg Digits, N-MNIST and Braille; only its 0.53 W figure is a vectorless Vivado estimate rather than a board reading, while the 175 MHz clock and the LUT and FF counts are implementation results. The route is drawn under keyword spotting, the nearest task chip, while the record's task is spoken-digit classification.

adaptive-fission-lynxi.name: Adaptive Fission to Lynxi HP201
adaptive-fission-lynxi.story: Adaptive Fission's post-training population expansion is measured for on-chip memory, seconds per evaluation epoch, and system watt-hours per epoch at batch size 32 on a physical Lynxi HP201 accelerator.
adaptive-fission-lynxi.note: Population coding is a post-training population expansion that replaces additional temporal integration with groups of binary sub-neurons carrying unequal fixed weights, applied on top of existing conversion methods including QCFS and SRP. The Lynxi HP201 is the commercial successor to Tianjic. Board sensors include peripherals, memory, and I/O, and the paper does not report per-sample latency or energy; closed interfaces prevent core-only measurement. Table 1 also contains unmodified no-Fission QCFS and SRP baseline rows.

py-spinnaker2-spinnaker2.name: py-spinnaker2 to SpiNNaker 2
py-spinnaker2-spinnaker2.story: A complex-valued Few-Spikes conversion and a hardware-aware fine-tuned spiking Q-network are both measured on physical single-chip SpiNNaker 2 boards against embedded-GPU baselines.
py-spinnaker2-spinnaker2.note: Neither record's own toolchain field names py-spinnaker2 directly, one says custom mapping to SpiNNaker2, the other custom SpiNNaker2 deployment, but the SpiNNaker runtime node's own summary independently names py-spinnaker2's experiment runner as the SpiNNaker-2 analogue of the SpiNNaker-1 execution pipeline, so the run step is grounded there rather than in either individual record. The Few-Spikes route serializes a temporal code rather than a firing rate; the Q-network route uses ordinary rate coding with subtractive reset.

dynap-se-tactile-chain.name: Custom configuration to DYNAP-SE
dynap-se-tactile-chain.story: An FBG-based e-skin drives an SNN mimicking early somatosensory processing on the physical DYNAP-SE mixed-signal analog chip, reaching a tactile localization error only 8 percent worse than software.
dynap-se-tactile-chain.note: The record names no reusable software framework, only a custom DYNAP-SE configuration, so the route reaches the chip directly. Median inference power is 185 microwatts and resting power is 8.7 microwatts, explicitly contrasted against an estimated milliwatt-class ARM implementation of the same dynamics.

eedn-corelet-truenorth.name: Corelet and EEDN to TrueNorth
eedn-corelet-truenorth.story: Eedn trains CNNs directly under TrueNorth's binary-neuron, trinary-synapse hardware constraints, and a live DVS128 camera stream feeds an Eedn-trained spiking CNN on physical TrueNorth silicon with no host-side frame accumulation.
eedn-corelet-truenorth.note: Eedn is constrained backprop training, not classical ANN-to-SNN conversion, mapping natively onto the chip's 23-parameter augmented IF neuron. The gesture-recognition deployment reaches 96.5 percent accuracy at 105 milliseconds gesture-onset latency and under 200 milliwatts, measured on a physical chip with a live camera feed. TrueNorth's global 1 kHz tick evaluates the whole network once per classification.

pynn-brainscales1.name: PyNN to BrainScaleS-1
pynn-brainscales1.story: Deep spiking networks converted from pretrained ANNs are benchmarked for accuracy and energy per inference across BrainScaleS, Spikey, and SpiNNaker, with hardware-in-the-loop retraining for the analog systems.
pynn-brainscales1.note: This map places the record only on BrainScaleS-1 among its three benchmarked platforms. SpiNNaker and Spikey energy figures are measured directly with real power meters; the BrainScaleS energy figure specifically is estimated from prior published per-synaptic-event data, not measured in this study, per the paper's own flag. PyNN's brainscales backend is the standard way this hardware is programmed.

pynn-spinnaker.name: PyNN to SpiNNaker
pynn-spinnaker.story: A fully closed-loop DVS-to-servo goalkeeper robot reaches 85 percent ball-interception accuracy at 6.5 milliseconds response latency on physical SpiNNaker, disconnected from any PC, and an earlier spiking deep belief network reaches 95 percent MNIST accuracy at under 0.3 watts on a single physical SpiNNaker 1 chip.
pynn-spinnaker.note: Cheng and Nikolic's own field, SpiNNaker native toolchain, is read as PyNN via sPyNNaker, the standard and essentially only way SpiNNaker is programmed, an authorized placement per Task 6's own record list. Stromatias et al. is placed on this same toolchain on different grounds. Its own toolchain field, SpiNNaker software stack, names no framework, and reading it as PyNN was an unstated inference that a controller review caught and reverted. Independent evidence for the compile stage survives that reversion. The route index's own spynnaker-to-spinnaker1 edge cites this paper by its own sources field, quoting the same 95.01 percent MNIST accuracy, 0.3 watt, and roughly 20 millisecond figures the paper reports, and site section 11.2 narrates it in prose alongside the sPyNNaker and SpiNNTools route description as an earlier, independent conversion. So the paper is placed by naming the compile and run chips, sPyNNaker and the SpiNNaker runtime, that this independent edge evidence supports, not by asserting a PyNN dev claim the record itself never makes.

spikingjelly-cri-fpga.name: SpikingJelly to CRI on FPGA
spikingjelly-cri-fpga.story: A SpikingJelly-trained DVS128 Gesture network, converted via hs_api to the CRI format, runs on physical CRI FPGA-based neuromorphic hardware with accuracy, clock cycles, and HBM accesses recorded per sample.
spikingjelly-cri-fpga.note: One of only a small handful of SpikingJelly-trained networks found to reach any physical chip, independent of the Lava or Loihi path. The network runs for 10 frames plus 6 drain steps per sample.

morphic-hdl.name: Custom HDL to MorphIC
morphic-hdl.story: MorphIC directly measures rate coding against rank-order coding energy cost for the same MNIST task on the same fabricated 65 nm chip.
morphic-hdl.note: The record names no reusable software framework beyond custom HDL synthesized in UMC 65 nm LP CMOS, so the route reaches the chip directly. Rate coding costs roughly 10 times more energy per classification than rank-order coding for near-equivalent accuracy on real fabricated silicon (205 microjoules versus 21.8 microjoules).

odin-hdl.name: Custom HDL to ODIN
odin-hdl.story: ODIN embeds rank-order-coded stochastic spike-driven on-chip learning, measured at 12.7 picojoules per synaptic operation and 84.5 percent MNIST accuracy on 9 fabricated 28 nm chips.
odin-hdl.note: The record names no reusable software framework beyond custom, open-source HDL, so the route reaches the chip directly. Energy per inference is 15 nanojoules, measured on fabricated silicon.

reckon-hdl.name: Custom HDL to ReckOn
reckon-hdl.story: ReckOn demonstrates end-to-end on-chip supervised learning over second-long timescales on 5 fabricated 28 nm chips, reaching 87.3 to 96.4 percent accuracy across three benchmarks.
reckon-hdl.note: The record names no reusable software framework beyond custom, open-source HDL, so the route reaches the chip directly. Peak efficiency is 5.3 picojoules per synaptic operation, measured on fabricated silicon.

ubrain-hdl.name: Custom HDL to uBrain
ubrain-hdl.story: uBrain, designed explicitly to ease ANN-to-SNN conversion for always-on edge inference, reaches 93.4 percent MNIST accuracy and 70 microwatts on a fabricated 40 nm prototype.
ubrain-hdl.note: The record names no reusable software framework beyond custom HDL in 40 nm CMOS, so the route reaches the chip directly. Energy per classification is 308 to 340 nanojoules, measured on the fabricated chip.

tianjic-native.name: Tianjic native toolchain
tianjic-native.story: Tianjic's shared axon, synapse, dendrite, soma, and router building blocks run both ANN and SNN modes on the same silicon, demonstrated driving an unmanned bicycle through simultaneous real-time perception and control.
tianjic-native.note: The record's own toolchain field is only a first-generation automatic model-mapping and compiling toolchain from Tsinghua, unnamed beyond that; it is not the same as BIDL, the commercial descendant toolchain the chip node's own summary separately names for Lynxi's later products, so no dev chip is asserted here. Throughput is 1.6 to 100 times and power efficiency is 12 to 10,000 times better than GPU baselines, measured hardware-in-the-loop, not in simulation.

syncnn-vitis.name: Vitis HLS or SDSoC to SyncNN
syncnn-vitis.story: SyncNN's synchronous reformulation of rate-encoded IF-neuron inference, proven mathematically equivalent to standard multi-timestep execution, reaches 99.6 percent MNIST accuracy at 13,086 frames per second across three physical Xilinx ARM-FPGA SoC boards.
syncnn-vitis.note: Built with the Vitis HLS and SDSoC hardware-mode flow. Reset is explicit, native reset by subtraction, Vm[o] minus Vth, and input is Poisson rate encoding, the closest FPGA match in this survey to QCFS-style IF-with-reset-by-subtraction-with-rate-coding assumptions.

cerebron-snntoolbox.name: SNN Toolbox to Cerebron
cerebron-snntoolbox.story: Cerebron's reconfigurable FPGA compute engine, explicitly built around the SNN Toolbox conversion methodology, reaches 99.40 percent MNIST accuracy at 0.026 milliseconds and 0.04 millijoules per image on a physical Xilinx XC7Z100 implementation.
cerebron-snntoolbox.note: Reset mode is inherited from SNN Toolbox's own convention, implying reset-by-subtraction, not independently restated in Cerebron's own text. A thinner MobileNet on CIFAR-10 reaches 91.90 percent at 10.63 milliseconds and 14.88 millijoules per image on the same physical implementation.

fpga-hls-general.name: FPGA HLS or RTL synthesis to FPGA accelerators
fpga-hls-general.story: FireFly v2 maps generalized multiplex-accumulate LIF dynamics onto DSP48E2 hard blocks at up to 600 MHz, and Spiker plus offers a library of six configurable neuron models with user-selectable hard or subtractive reset, both measured on physical Xilinx FPGA boards.
fpga-hls-general.note: FireFly v2's own toolchain field is custom HDL for Xilinx UltraScale DSP48E2, naming no training framework. Spiker plus's own toolchain field is BPTT-trainable via snnTorch or offline-trained, so snnTorch is asserted only for that record's own via, not as the toolchain's default line. Spiker plus is the first accelerator surveyed with reset by subtraction as an explicit, user-selectable configuration, matching QCFS-style IF-with-reset-by-subtraction.

hxtorch-brainscales2.name: hxtorch to BrainScaleS-2
hxtorch-brainscales2.story: hxtorch's non-spiking hagen mode executes matmul and convolution primitives directly on physical BrainScaleS-2 silicon as analog vector-matrix multiplication, already traced in Section 11 with no separate E1 paper record of its own.
hxtorch-brainscales2.note: This toolchain exists so the chip answers a click even without an attached paper. BrainScaleS-2's native AdEx circuit performs a hard reset, clamped to the reset potential for a refractory period on spike; no source describes a native or multi-compartment-workaround reset-by-subtraction mode. Physical analog circuit time runs at roughly 1000 times biological acceleration.

hand-designed-loihi1.name: Hand-designed microcode to Loihi 1
hand-designed-loihi1.story: A one-shot local-plasticity olfactory-bulb-model circuit and a hand-designed head-direction SLAM circuit both reach physical Loihi silicon as hand-designed microcode rather than through any training framework.
hand-designed-loihi1.note: Neither record names a framework at all, so dev, export, and compile are null and the route reaches Loihi 1 directly. The olfaction circuit reaches 2.75 milliseconds and 0.43 millijoules per sniff; a 2023 replication study found the underlying dataset suffers from sensor drift and a non-randomized protocol, and that a simple hash-table baseline matches or beats it under proper train and test splitting, which undercuts the algorithmic claim without invalidating the hardware measurement. The SLAM circuit reaches 100 times less dynamic power than GMapping on CPU at comparable localization accuracy.

stbp-loihi-sddpg.name: Custom STBP to Loihi
stbp-loihi-sddpg.story: A spiking actor network co-trained end to end with a deep critic via a custom STBP extension is deployed on Loihi for real-world TurtleBot2 mapless navigation, using 75 times less energy per inference than DDPG on a Jetson TX2.
stbp-loihi-sddpg.note: The record names only a custom STBP extension, no reusable named tool, so dev is null and the direct-training-surrogate-gradient learning chip carries the claim instead. Measured on a physical 2-chip Kapoho Bay board.

pytorch-nxsdk-lava-loihi.name: PyTorch to NxSDK or Lava
pytorch-nxsdk-lava-loihi.story: An SNN policy trained via spiking reinforcement learning in PyTorch simulation is ported to both physical Loihi 1 and physical Loihi 2 for an industrial peg-in-hole insertion task with a KUKA arm.
pytorch-nxsdk-lava-loihi.note: One toolchain with two targets, not two separate toolchains, because this is one experiment reported once, with the Loihi 1 leg runs through NxSDK, the Loihi 2 leg through Lava. PyTorch itself is a generic training library, not a named SNN-specific tool, so dev is left null here, the same treatment given the custom STBP extension in sddpg. Dynamic energy on Loihi 2 is 53 plus or minus 17 microjoules per inference versus about 3800 microjoules on CPU and roughly 100s of microjoules on GPU.

modified-microcode-loihi2.name: Modified microcode to Loihi 2
modified-microcode-loihi2.story: An ANN converted to a Sigma-Delta Neural Network using Loihi 2's native graded spikes, 16-bit signed-integer payload activation deltas, is measured for latency, throughput, power, energy per frame, and energy-delay product on an in-house 16-chip Intel Loihi 2 VPX development board.
modified-microcode-loihi2.note: The record names only nxkernel 0.3.0 with modified Loihi 2 microcode, a custom, non-reusable tool, so dev, export, and compile are null. Host-side input-delta generation and output accumulation or decoding remain outside the neurocores, and the Jetson comparison uses whole-SoC power and is not boundary-identical.

mlgenn-eventprop-netx-loihi2.name: mlGeNN EventProp to NetX
mlgenn-eventprop-netx-loihi2.story: mlGeNN's EventProp exact-gradient training with learned synaptic delays, deployed via NetX to a physical single-chip Loihi 2, reaches 1.46 to 1.54 millisecond latency and 0.21 to 0.46 millijoule energy for keyword spotting, 18 times faster and 250 times less energy than a Jetson Orin Nano at batch 1.
mlgenn-eventprop-netx-loihi2.note: Distinct from mlGeNN's own separate GPU-only leg (mlgenn-to-genn-cuda) and from the lava-dl-based slayer-loihi2 toolchain, since this record's own dev tool is mlGeNN, not lava-dl. The learning chip is spike-time-gradient-methods, not the generic surrogate-gradient chip, because this survey's own text identifies EventProp specifically as an exact spike-time gradient method structurally distinct from surrogate-gradient BPTT.

slayer-nxtf-loihi1.name: SLAYER to NxTF
slayer-nxtf-loihi1.story: A SLAYER-trained CNN deployed via NxTF and NxSDK on a physical Loihi board measures latency and energy for DVS Gesture with performance probes built into the deployment script.
slayer-nxtf-loihi1.note: NxTF successfully compiles this SLAYER-trained network for physical Loihi 1 execution, in contrast to the SpikingJelly-to-NxTF route this map documents as broken at the same compiler stage. SLAYER here is the standalone training library, predating and distinct from its later home inside Lava-DL, so dev is slayer, not lava-dl.

snntorch-portenta-h7.name: snnTorch to a C runtime on an Arduino Portenta H7
snntorch-portenta-h7.story: An snnTorch-trained LIF network with spike-driven pruning is exported to a statically-allocated C runtime and measured on a physical Arduino Portenta H7, reaching a 7.4 to 7.5 times speedup over the snnTorch Python baseline on ST-MNIST.
snntorch-portenta-h7.note: Direct surrogate-gradient training, not an ANN-to-SNN conversion. N-MNIST supplies address-event input from a DVS event camera; ST-MNIST supplies tactile spike events, carried on the sensor and input capability lines rather than the drawn default, which follows the primary N-MNIST case. The paper also benchmarks the same C runtime on a desktop CPU, not drawn here since the Portenta H7 is the physical MCU target.

memory-decoupled-cortex-m.name: Memory-decoupled event-driven SNN on a Cortex-M MCU
memory-decoupled-cortex-m.story: A double-depth rolling array decouples SNN timestep unrolling from memory footprint on an STM32H7 Cortex-M7 MCU, cutting peak dynamic SRAM overhead by about 74 percent and reaching 197.69 milliseconds and 76.98 millijoules per inference on a physical board for a recurrent MNIST SNN.
memory-decoupled-cortex-m.note: The record's own toolchain field is not found, a custom hardware-software co-optimization framework whose training toolchain is not stated in the retrieved abstract, so dev, export, compile, and run are all left unnamed rather than inferred. The target chip is the map's existing generic Cortex-M MCU node, already deliberately generic since its first paper's own exact part is unnamed; this STM32H7 Cortex-M7 record sits in the same family and gives that chip its second route. Only the abstract and metadata page were retrieved, IEEE Xplore full text is paywalled, so no task, sensor, or code chip is drawn beyond what the abstract itself states.

tensorflow-lite-stedgeai-stm32n6.name: TensorFlow Lite to STEdgeAI to an STM32N6 NPU
tensorflow-lite-stedgeai-stm32n6.story: A TensorFlow-Lite-trained LIF network, quantized by STMicroelectronics' STEdgeAI toolchain, runs on the STM32N657X0's integrated Neural-ART NPU 7.6 times faster and at under a quarter the energy per sample of the same board's Cortex-M55 CPU path.
tensorflow-lite-stedgeai-stm32n6.note: Both the NPU and the comparator Cortex-M55 CPU execution path are measured on the same physical board in the same degree project; only the NPU path is drawn here as the toolchain's own named target. Dataset, task, and timestep count are not found in the retrieved text, so no task or code chip is drawn.

tensorflow-coral-edgetpu.name: TensorFlow to a Coral Edge TPU
tensorflow-coral-edgetpu.story: A DAVIS240C event camera feeds a TensorFlow-trained tracking and path-prediction network on the physical Google Coral Edge TPU dev board, reaching 4 milliseconds latency and 1.72 watts against 27 milliseconds and 5.48 watts for the same network on an Intel Compute Stick measured in the same paper.
tensorflow-coral-edgetpu.note: The record's own toolchain field names only TensorFlow deploying directly to the Coral Edge TPU Dev Board's 8-bit fixed-point path, with no separate compiler stage stated, so TensorFlow is carried on the run step rather than split into dev and compile stages it does not name, the same pattern this map already uses for a framework's own runtime executing directly on a target (PyTorch's CUDA backend, GeNN's generated CUDA). The record's own neuron and reset fields are not found, and its title's spike-based wording refers to the DAVIS240C sensor's address-event input rather than to a stated spiking neuron model, so its standing as a spiking deployment is qualified rather than asserted outright; no code or neuron chip is drawn.

northpole-npu.name: Custom digital NPU compiler to NorthPole
northpole-npu.story: IBM NorthPole, a purely digital, low-precision spatial-dataflow inference accelerator with no spiking or event-driven neuron model, runs YOLOv4 object detection and ResNet-50 image classification on physical fabricated 12 nanometer silicon, measured against GPU and CPU baselines.
northpole-npu.note: The record's own toolchain field is generic, a custom digital NPU compiler naming no reusable framework, so dev, export, compile, and run are all left unnamed rather than inferred. NorthPole is a boundary case for this survey, non-spiking with no neuron, reset, or encoding fields that apply; it carries the NPU chip on the strength of a shared TrueNorth lineage rather than as a spiking deployment, per site section 5.3. The same paper also measures ResNet-50 image classification on the same physical chip; only the object-detection task is drawn, since this map's object-detection application otherwise carries no physical route at all.

image-classification-static.note: Image classification is the most physically confirmed task on this map. SNN Toolbox's threshold-balancing conversion reaches 98.20 percent MNIST accuracy on physical SpiNNaker 1, Sinabs's direct BPTT training reaches 98.50 percent on N-MNIST on physical Speck1, Quartz's time-to-first-spike conversion is measured for static power, dynamic power, latency, energy, and energy-delay product on physical Loihi 1, and mlGeNN's rate-based and few-spike conversion of VGG-16 and ResNet-20 runs as GeNN-generated CUDA on a physical GPU.

object-detection.note: One surveyed object-detection deployment now carries physical evidence on this task, though it is a boundary case. IBM NorthPole, a non-spiking low-precision digital NPU with no membrane-potential dynamics, runs YOLOv4 object detection on physical fabricated silicon; the survey carries it as a conventional NPU target on the strength of a shared TrueNorth lineage rather than as a spiking deployment. Spiking-YOLO's own conversion still reports GPU simulation accuracy only, at evidence class E5, not a measurement on any of this map's carried targets.

gesture-recognition.note: The surveyed gesture-recognition deployments span a converted DVS-camera network measured on physical Loihi 1 at 89.64 percent accuracy and 11.43 milliseconds of per-frame latency with events pre-accumulated into frames before conversion, a directly trained dynamic SNN on physical Speck reaching real-time power as low as 0.70 milliwatts, a live DVS128 stream feeding an Eedn-trained network on physical TrueNorth with no host-side frame accumulation at 96.5 percent accuracy and 105 milliseconds latency, a SLAYER-trained network deployed via NxTF on physical Loihi 1, and a SpikingJelly-trained network converted via hs_api to physical CRI FPGA-based neuromorphic hardware.

tracking-motion.note: One surveyed tracking deployment now carries physical evidence on this task. A DAVIS240C event camera feeds a TensorFlow-trained tracking and path-prediction network on the physical Google Coral Edge TPU dev board at 4 milliseconds latency and 1.72 watts, though the record's own neuron and reset fields are unstated, so its standing as a spiking deployment is qualified rather than asserted outright.

keyword-spotting-audio.note: Both surveyed keyword-spotting-adjacent deployments are directly trained rather than converted. Rockpool's mapping to Xylo Audio 2 reaches 95.31 percent deployed accuracy at 216 to 298 microwatts, and FeNN's RISC-V vector processor runs an adaptive-LIF spoken-digit classifier faster than a similar model on Loihi and twice as fast as an embedded GPU at half the energy, though the FeNN record's own task is spoken-digit classification rather than keyword spotting proper.

biosignal-decoding.note: No surveyed run with physical evidence on this task is on the map yet. This survey's audited electromyography and electroencephalography deployments on physical Loihi and Loihi 2 are not among this map's carried routes.

olfaction.note: Imam and Cleland's one-shot olfactory-bulb-model circuit reaches physical Loihi silicon at 2.75 milliseconds and 0.43 millijoules per sniff through hand-designed microcode. A 2023 replication study found the underlying dataset suffers from sensor drift and a non-randomized protocol, and that a simple hash-table baseline matches or beats the network's accuracy under proper train and test splitting; the hardware measurement itself stands, but the algorithmic claim is substantially undercut.

robotics-closed-loop-control.note: Three surveyed robotics deployments now carry physical evidence on this map, a PyTorch-trained spiking policy ported to both Loihi 1 via NxSDK and Loihi 2 via Lava for an industrial peg-in-hole insertion task, a custom-STBP-trained spiking actor network on Loihi for real-world TurtleBot2 mapless navigation at 75 times less energy per inference than DDPG on a Jetson TX2, and a DVS-to-SpiNNaker-to-servo goalkeeper robot, fully closed-loop and disconnected from any PC, intercepting balls up to 1 meter per second at 85 percent accuracy.

slam.note: Tang et al.'s hand-designed, biologically constrained head-direction circuit reaches physical Loihi silicon at 100 times less dynamic power than GMapping on CPU, at comparable localization accuracy, through hand-designed microcode rather than any training framework.

optimization-constraint-satisfaction.note: No surveyed run with physical evidence on this task is on the map yet. The audited constraint-satisfaction and sparse-coding circuits reach physical Loihi silicon through hand-designed microcode, a software route this map does not carry.

classical-conversion.text: ANN-to-SNN conversion trains a conventional ANN by ordinary backpropagation and only afterward re-expresses each unit's activation as an integrate-and-fire neuron's spike count under a stated correspondence, so the non-differentiable spiking threshold is never encountered by the optimizer.

low-latency-conversion.text: Low-latency conversion targets the finite-time error a short simulation horizon creates by pulling one of three levers, reshaping the ANN's own activation function, calibrating or redesigning the spiking neuron, or changing the spike encoding, rather than by simply lengthening the horizon.

quant-aware-conversion.text: Quantization-aware conversion trains the ANN's own activation function to anticipate the discretization grid before conversion happens, an ordinary quantization-aware training step applied to the ANN rather than a hardware intervention.

codesigned-conversion.text: Hardware-aware conversion maps a network onto a specific platform, and every confirmed instance in the audited corpus of a paper that both proposes a conversion method and reports its own physical-silicon measurement abandons rate coding for a code native to the target platform.

direct-training-surrogate-gradient.text: A surrogate-gradient method keeps the exact binary spiking forward pass fixed and substitutes a smooth surrogate derivative for the Heaviside derivative on the backward pass, so that automatic differentiation has a nonzero local sensitivity to propagate at every step.

spike-time-gradient-methods.text: Exact spike-time gradient methods, including EXODUS and EventProp, differentiate analytically through the timing of the spike-generation event itself rather than substituting a surrogate slope for the same crossing.

local-learning-plasticity.text: A local learning rule updates a synaptic weight from quantities already available at that synapse, typically the relative timing or recent history of the presynaptic and postsynaptic events, rather than from a loss gradient propagated backward through every later layer and step.

hand-designed-hybrid-finetuning.text: A hand-designed hybrid method applies a hand-designed correction before deployment rather than during training, as when a mapless-navigation policy trained end to end by gradient descent is passed through a Loihi-specific eight-bit integer weight-rescaling step before its corrected weights are measured on physical Loihi.

hardware-in-the-loop-training.text: Hardware-in-the-loop training is the most literal sense of online learning in the audited evidence, because the forward pass executes on the physical target device at every training iteration rather than on a simulator standing in for it.

hybrid-finetuning.text: Hybrid fine-tuning corrects a converted network's activation statistics after conversion, calibrating bias, weight, and initial membrane potential statistics against residual, reset, clipping, and discretization error without altering the underlying rate-matching correspondence.

rate-coding.text: Rate coding represents a scalar as a sequence of binary events whose spike count or firing fraction over the window the decoder reads back, with quantization error that scales as one over T for deterministic counting and one over the square root of T for stochastic Poisson coding.

ttfs.text: Time-to-first-spike coding maps a scalar to the latency of a single spike relative to a reference onset, with each neuron firing at most once and larger values producing earlier spikes.

phase-coding.text: Phase coding assigns each spike a weight given by its position within a repeating cycle of K timesteps, typically the powers of two, so the decoder sums the weights of the phases at which a spike occurred.

burst-coding.text: Burst coding uses the same spike-count mechanism as rate coding but permits a neuron to emit more than one spike within a single timestep when its residual post-threshold membrane potential remains large.

population-coding.text: Population coding distributes a represented value across the activity pattern of a population of neurons rather than through any single neuron's rate or timing, paying its cost in neurons rather than in steps.

sigma-delta.text: Sigma-delta coding emits a spike only when the change in activation since the last transmission exceeds a threshold, and that spike carries the size of the change as its payload rather than a count of unit events.

rank-order-coding.text: Rank order coding discards magnitude entirely and encodes only the relative order in which a population's neurons fire during one feedforward wave, decoded by a shunting-inhibition mechanism in which each arriving spike desensitizes the postsynaptic neuron by its arrival rank.

direct-input-encoding.text: Direct coding is strictly an input convention rather than a spike code, applying a real-valued input as a constant analog current to a layer's neurons at every step rather than producing a spike train.

binary-spikes.text: A general event can carry an address, a timestamp, a polarity or type, and an optional payload, and the bare binary spike is one important special case of that general event.

signed-spikes.text: A signed spike lets a neuron fire a positive or a negative spike on crossing a threshold in either direction, expanding the representable range beyond a single nonnegative spike count.

graded-spikes.text: A graded spike payload exists only on Loihi 2, up to 32 bits per event, while every other audited platform carries a binary event whatever its native neuron model.

if-neuron.text: Integrate-and-fire is the baseline neuron model, its synaptic stage has no memory, its membrane stage adds the current to the previous state with no decay, and its threshold is fixed, the target the classical ANN-to-SNN conversion literature relies on when it equates a spike count with a rectified linear unit activation.

lif-neuron.text: Leaky integrate-and-fire keeps the trivial synaptic stage of IF but introduces a per-layer leak factor so the membrane relaxes toward its resting value between inputs instead of holding charge indefinitely.

cuba-lif.text: Current-based LIF gives the synaptic stage genuine memory by making it a leaky integrator of the incoming weighted events rather than an instantaneous sum, and it is documented as Loihi's native default neuron dynamics and as sPyNNaker's documented default cell type.

adaptive-neuron.text: Adaptive LIF couples the threshold itself to the neuron's own recent spiking, raising it after every spike and letting it relax back toward a baseline between spikes, so a constant input no longer produces a constant firing rate.

multi-compartment.text: A multi-compartment neuron generalizes the single state triple into several coupled instances, and on Loihi a second compartment is documented as the way both a subtractive reset and spike-frequency adaptation are recovered from a hardware primitive whose native single-compartment behavior does neither.

pasc-if.text: PASC-IF is the precise ANN-SNN conversion integrate-and-fire formulation PASCAL builds its sensitivity-assigned per-layer resolution onto, which APEX and NeuroFlex synthesize in RTL simulation rather than fabricate as measured silicon.

reset-by-subtraction.text: Reset-by-subtraction removes only the threshold that was just crossed and carries the residual charge forward into the next step, removing the systematic input-dependent bias that reset-to-zero introduces.

reset-to-zero.text: Reset-to-zero clamps the post-reset state to a fixed baseline, usually zero, whenever an event is emitted, discarding the residual charge by which the pre-reset candidate exceeded threshold.

sync-tick.text: A synchronization barrier holds every part of a system at the same algorithmic step until all parts have finished it, the mechanism Loihi, TrueNorth, and Tianjic each use to advance a single global algorithmic timestep across an entire chip despite asynchronous computation inside a core.

async-events.text: Asynchronous event time is the absence of any synchronization barrier, so that a component acts as soon as its own input arrives, the timestep-free execution style of a substrate such as Speck2e where state updates occur strictly on event arrival.

analog-time.text: An analog or mixed-signal system realizes neuron and synapse dynamics as physical circuit behavior evolving in continuous time, typically at a fixed acceleration factor relative to biological or wall-clock time, rather than as a discrete-time numerical recurrence.

single-pass.text: On Akida's standard QuantizeML-to-CNN2SNN route there is no user-exposed multi-timestep simulation horizon, so the mapped network evaluates in a single feedforward pass with no membrane potential carried across timesteps.

silicon-cochlea.why: No carried toolchain's sensor field or route-index edge names a silicon cochlea; the FeNN spoken-digit classifier this map draws under keyword spotting consumes cochlea-model spike trains rather than a silicon cochlea sensor.

imu-analog-sensor.why: No carried toolchain's sensor field or route-index edge names an IMU or other analog sensor; the audited robotics and SLAM records reach Loihi through hand-designed microcode or custom training pipelines outside this map's named routes.

hand-designed-hybrid-finetuning.why: No attached record draws this chip as its learning value; Tang et al.'s mapless-navigation policy, attached to Quartz to Loihi 1 under surrogate-gradient training, also applies a hand-designed, Loihi-specific eight-bit weight-rescaling correction step that this map does not separately draw.

hybrid-finetuning.why: No carried toolchain attaches a hybrid ANN-plus-SNN deployment; NengoLoihi's hybrid model reaching physical Loihi 1 is not one of this map's carried routes.

phase-coding.why: No carried toolchain's code field or attached record uses phase coding; the survey documents it as a software or training-time convention layered on an ordinary binary-spike substrate rather than as an exercised hardware route.

burst-coding.why: No carried toolchain's code field or attached record uses burst coding; Speck documents a multi-spike-per-step mode, but the deployment cited alongside it used a plain single-spike neuron instead.

direct-input-encoding.why: No carried toolchain's code field uses direct constant-current input as its neural code; the robotics policies that use it feed continuous sensor state directly through pipelines outside this map's named software routes.

signed-spikes.why: No carried toolchain's payload field or attached record uses a signed spike; Fast-SNN cites Loihi's documented support for signed spikes only as design justification and reports no execution on that or any other chip.

pasc-if.why: No carried toolchain attaches a PASC-IF record; PASCAL and APEX synthesize the PASC-IF neuron in RTL simulation rather than on any of this map's named hardware targets.

norse.why: No carried toolchain's dev field names Norse; it appears in the audited evidence only as a comparator framework benchmarked against SpikingJelly's training speed, not as a route this map draws.

nengo.why: No carried toolchain's dev field names Nengo; NengoLoihi's hybrid ANN-plus-SNN deployment to physical Loihi 1 is not one of this map's carried routes.

brian2.why: No carried toolchain's dev field names Brian2; SNN Toolbox can export to it as an internal simulator backend, evidenced only at E5 in software, not as a route this map draws to physical silicon.

bidl.why: No carried toolchain's dev field names BIDL; this survey's audited evidence does not attach a deployment record to it.

backend-graph.why: backend-graph is a generic intermediate node in the route index that several toolchains pass through internally, but none of this map's carried toolchains names it as its own drawn export stage.

nengo-loihi.why: No carried toolchain's compile field names NengoLoihi; its hybrid ANN-plus-SNN deployment to physical Loihi 1 is not one of this map's carried routes.

ann2snn.why: No carried toolchain's compile field names ann2snn; this survey's audited evidence does not attach a deployment record to it.

host-io.why: Host encoding and readout is a universal, implicit stage this survey's contract names for every audited platform, but none of this map's carried toolchains draws it as its own explicit run step.

lava-loihi-sim.why: No carried toolchain targets the Lava Loihi simulator; the Loihi routes this map carries target physical Loihi 1 or Loihi 2 silicon, not the simulator.

xylo-sim.why: No carried toolchain targets the Xylo simulator; Rockpool to Xylo on this map targets physical Xylo Audio 2 silicon, not the simulator.

akida-sim.why: No carried toolchain targets the Akida software backend; QuantizeML to CNN2SNN to Akida on this map targets physical AKD1000, AKD1500, or Akida Pico silicon, not the simulator.

hxtorch-sim.why: No carried toolchain targets hxtorch simulation; the audited hxtorch route targets physical BrainScaleS-2 silicon in its non-spiking hagen mode, and is not one of this map's carried routes.

fpga-truenorth-emulation.why: No carried toolchain targets TrueNorth FPGA emulation; the audited Eedn plus Corelet route reaches physical TrueNorth silicon directly, a target this map does not carry.

apex.why: No carried toolchain targets APEX; APEX synthesizes the PASC-IF neuron in RTL simulation rather than reaching a target this map carries.

neuroflex.why: No carried toolchain targets NeuroFlex; NeuroFlex synthesizes its column-level PASC-IF scheduler in RTL simulation rather than reaching a target this map carries.

lynxi-ka200.why: No carried toolchain targets Lynxi KA200; the audited SpikingJelly-to-Lynxi edge is evidenced at E3, and Adaptive Fission's own physical measurement targets the Lynxi HP201 successor chip, neither of which is one of this map's carried routes.

dynapcnn.why: No carried toolchain targets DYNAP-CNN as its own endpoint; Sinabs to Speck on this map compiles through the DynapCNN mapper but targets the Speck chip itself.

dynap-se2.why: No carried toolchain targets DYNAP-SE2; this survey's audited evidence locates no rate-coded ANN-to-SNN conversion pipeline for it.

innatera-pulsar.why: No carried toolchain targets Innatera Pulsar; every quantitative figure this survey located for it is vendor-sourced without an independent peer-reviewed benchmark.
